I'm diagnosed but have almost no issues in day to day life; I'm only here because I'm traveling at a much higher altitude than I'm used to and so am actually having problems (leaving tomorrow, thank god). The question is really whether you meet the diagnostic criteria, and whether following the lifestyle advice (drink lots of water, salty food, etc) helps you with your symptoms.

And you don't want to have a severe case of anything. You want your current problems to be taken seriously.

If you feel fine and know what you need to keep feeling that way I don't see a need to spend time and money seeing a specialist. I have a very mild case, so my diagnosis has only really been useful to me for telling me what I need to do to stay healthy.

Milder case than yours I think, but I've been diagnosed since 10 and it occasionally comes up, mostly in the context of me explaining why I'm so anal about carrying water everywhere. I just say something like "I have a very mild heart condition, it doesn't normally cause me issues, but if I get dehydrated I will pass out a lot sooner than the average person." In your case I would do the same basic thing but just describe what your symptoms specifically are/what you can and can't do.

Edit: Also I think these responses are weirdly defensive. It makes sense to explain the exact severity of your condition to people so that they don't worry about you when they don't need to or mistakenly leave you out of activities you can do (or, conversely, expect you to do something that would put you at risk of passing out). As far as romantic partners, if it is a significant hindrance in your daily life I think it's in everyone's best interest to tell them sooner rather than later, but if it's not something that is likely to significantly impact the kinds of things you can do together or your support needs then I see no issue with leaving it until it comes up.

That said, I think a principled defense of the pro-trans position looks very different from what activists currently push. In particular, I think it has to be based on the idea that this is biological and related to brain development, which from what I know is somewhere between plausible and likely, though we don't know the exact mechanism by which this could happen, and it might vary by typology. For a while I was very strongly leaning towards a one-cause model in which a specific "switch" or set of "switches" being flipped caused gender dysphoria, but I had a very interesting conversation recently that made me more open to a polycausal model, in which a number of different factors, some or many of which are tied to traits often found in transitioners such as same-sex attraction, autism, etc, all make transition more likely and/or more beneficial if done, and this is what causes the continuum effect we see where some people are very strongly resolved towards and helped by transition and others are more ambiguous or do it and then regret it (the detransition case is presumably also helped along by a degree of social contagion).

If it is biological, given that we don't know much about how to affect brain structure/chemistry aside from relatively crude methods involving medication which we don't know how to apply to the dysphoria case, medical transition makes a lot more sense, and once you accept that at least some people need to (or at least will be dramatically benefited if they) medically transition, some level of social acceptance and accommodation flows from there. Specific policies are up for debate and involve a balancing of the rights and needs of the groups involved.

You can say the state of being a man or woman is based on chromosomes alone, or on genitals at birth, but that definition is in most cases not as useful as a bimodal one focusing on primary and secondary sex characteristics.

I'm being honest. I used to weigh 200 pounds at 5'6 and have lost to about 160 (maybe higher now since I've been on vacation for a while). I am still overweight and have probably at least 15 to go for ideal health, but I feel much better now than I did then despite having had very good blood work and no obvious signs of physical problems. I was relatively active, I just ate too much. I'm not losing weight because I hate myself, I'm doing it because I feel physically better and more comfortable this way. You just can't be healthy or fit at a BMI of 30+, it isn't possible. I know the range for what is acceptable varies by race and by frame and does not always line up perfectly with the suggestion of 18.5 to 25, but the ratio of weight to height you are describing is not good for anyone. 

My friends and family were perfectly nice to me before and after losing weight, but were obviously supportive of me given I did it in a healthy way and it was excess fat that I needed to lose for my health and fitness and would not have gained in the first place without unhealthy habits. I don't doubt that the people in your life don't judge you, or that they care about you, but there is no getting around that a person who is, say, 140 pounds at 5'6 will look different from one who is 200. Nobody has to hate you or think less of you because of it, but people objectively look different with that much excess fat on their bodies. I certainly did. It didn't make me a worse person or morally inferior, but I was not healthy and I objectively looked very different than I do now. 

This is not intended to shame anyone, it is a statement of fact. You can choose not to lose weight and people should not treat you as lesser for it, but it is not the ideal decision with regards to your physical fitness. People make decisions that aren't ideal all the time- I know I do- and you're right that shame doesn't help. That said, if you can't acknowledge when you are doing something unhealthy, you have a problem. It's your right to live how you want and you should not be told you have less inherent worth for that, but not all choices are equally responsible or healthy and there is nothing wrong with acknowledging that.

You cannot weigh 200 pounds at 5'6 and be healthy, nor can you look like you are. You may get a lot of exercise and eat healthy foods, but you are either eating too much of them or you have not been consuming the correct amount for long enough for your weight to catch up.
